pass_b_english: (What one must do, he has said.) “O rivers and earth, and you who beneath punish worn-out men, whoever should swear a false oath: you be witnesses, and complete the song for us. I came consulting, that I may arrive into the land of Telemachus, whom I left upon a nurse’s bosom, my child.” For such was the best incantation.

(What one must chant, he says.) “Hear me, kindly-smiling and overseer, well-sowing Anubis [lock crux unrestored] … Come, Hermes, snatcher; here, well-tressed chthonic Zeus; [lock unrestored] fulfill this incantation. Here, Hades and Chthon, unquenchable fire, Helios Titan; come also Ia and Phtha and Phre [lock unrestored], and much-honored Nephtho and much-blessed Ablanatho, fire-dragon-girded, earth-drawer, ibis-named, Abrasax, far-famed daemon of the cosmic name, allotting axis and chorion and lights, all-father of the Bears; come also, in mastery more excellent than all, to me, Phren, [lock crux unrestored] and Genea and Apebiota and beautifully-burning Fire; come, Isis chthonic and heavenly and who rule over dreams, and Sirius who …”

And these things I shouted, standing beside the pit; for I remembered well Circe’s instructions, who knows as many drugs as the wide earth nourishes. And a great wave came of lion-fighting Acheron, Cocytus and Lethe and greatest Pyriphlegethon, and a fleet of the dead stood around also beside the pit; and first came the soul of Elpenor the companion. (And the things next.) Either, then, being thus, the poet himself kept silent the rest of the overcurious incantation because of the dignity of the subject, or the Peisistratids, stitching the other verses together, split these off, judging them alien to the line of the poetry there [lock crux unrestored]. As a more costly offspring of an incantation I myself arranged it here.

This whole hypothesis, laid up, you will find both in the archives of the ancient fatherland-colony Aelia Capitolina of Palestine and at Nysa in Caria, and through the thirteenth in Rome, toward Alexander’s baths, in the beautiful library in the Pantheon which I myself architected for the Augustus. Julius Africanus, Cestus 18.
From the Cesti of Africanus, which is Cestus 13, chapter 22: simple purgatives. Juice of cyclamen smeared on the navel is a vigorous purgative. And the summer cleansing is this:
